Calcium. Element 20, Ca. An alkaline-earth metal that is essential to nearly all living organisms. It functions as a structural component of bones and teeth, and as a critical signaling ion in neurons and muscle cells. The body tightly regulates calcium levels through vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and dietary intake.

Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust at 3.7 percent, found primarily as calcium carbonate—limestone and chalk—and as calcium phosphate, which is the mineral phase of bone. It has atomic number 20 with an electron configuration that readily loses two valence electrons to form calcium cations with a two-plus charge. These are stable and inert.

About 99 percent of the calcium in your body is stored in bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate compound that provides strength and hardness. The remaining one percent exists as free or protein-bound calcium ions in blood and cells. The body controls serum calcium tightly—between 8.5 and 10.5 milligrams per deciliter—because deviations disrupt cellular function.

Calcium ions are the primary trigger for muscle contraction. When calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, they bind calmodulin, which allows the myosin-actin interaction that makes muscles work. In neurons, calcium ions flowing into the cell through voltage-gated calcium channels trigger the release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft.

Vitamin D, also called calcitriol, stimulates calcium absorption in the small intestine. Parathyroid hormone increases blood calcium by promoting the kidneys to reabsorb it and by promoting bone resorption. Milk and dairy products are rich sources of dietary calcium. Vegetables like kale and spinach contain calcium, but they also contain oxalates that reduce how much of the calcium your body can actually use.
